messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Captain David Tavita still remembers the weight of the helicopter door sliding shut. It was 0430 hours, the same time of day that now, thirty-five years later, makes his chest tighten before he even opens his eyes. He was a young Marine pilot then, ferrying a squad through the dense jungle canopy of an island chain he had never heard of before deployment. What he remembers most clearly is not the explosion itself—the RPG that punched through the floor panel—but the texture of the hydraulic fluid that sprayed across his hands afterward. Thick, warm, and syrupy, it coated his flight gloves and soaked into the fabric. He can still feel it. That specific viscosity, that smell of burnt metal and hot oil, returns to him without warning in the most ordinary moments. A spilled soda on the counter. The grease on a restaurant napkin. His wife’s hand lotion if it is too heavy. Suddenly he is back in the cockpit, the helicopter shuddering, the crew chief screaming, and the terror floods through him as fresh as if it were happening now.

David is sixty-three years old, a married man who has flown commercial airliners for three decades. He has logged more than twenty thousand hours in the air without incident. But the sound of a helicopter—even one on the news, even one miles away—can derail an entire day. He has learned to keep his office door closed at the hangar. He avoids the tarmac when the medevac choppers are running drills. His colleagues think he is particular about noise. The truth is that he is certain the sound will pull him under, that the memory will seize him by the throat and he will lose control in front of everyone.

The memory itself feels strange to him, like a story that happened to someone else. He can narrate the facts: the extraction gone wrong, the two Marines who did not make it, the medal he never wore. But when he tries to place himself inside that cockpit, something in his mind resists. It is as though the man who lived through that night is a stranger. And yet, when the trigger comes without warning—when a sudden movement from a passenger boarding the plane makes him flinch, or when he walks into a briefing room and finds himself counting the exits before he can stop himself—the terror is undeniably his own. It belongs to him in a way the memory does not. That contradiction hollows him out.

He has come to believe that there is something fundamentally wrong with him. Other pilots from his unit went on with their lives. They have barbecues and grandchildren and hobbies. David used to be a happy man. He remembers laughing easily, joking with the crew, looking forward to layovers in foreign cities. Now he is miserable in a way that feels permanent. He does not trust the world. He scans every restaurant, every waiting room, every hotel lobby for the nearest way out. Night is worse. He has not slept through the night in years. He lies awake listening for sounds that are not there, his body braced, his mind running through emergency procedures for threats that do not exist.

His wife has stopped asking why he paces the bedroom at 0430. She knows better than to touch him when he is standing at the window. The marriage has narrowed into a careful choreography of unspoken rules. He cannot explain to her why a certain restaurant booth is unbearable, why he needs to sit facing the door, why he sometimes leaves the table mid-meal because a texture on the napkin has sent him reeling. He has stopped trying. What would he say? That the world is dangerous and he is the only one who sees it clearly? That he is broken in a way that cannot be fixed?

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in the cockpit last month. A passenger made a sudden lurching movement during turbulence, and David’s hands went white on the yoke. His first officer asked if he was all right. David said yes. But he was not all right. He was back in the jungle, and the terror was absolute, and for a few seconds he could not remember which war he was in. That night he told his wife he would make an appointment. He does not know if anything can change. He is afraid that the memory will always feel like someone else’s, and that the terror will always feel like his own. But he is more afraid of what will happen if he does nothing.
